title: Given items with weights and values and a capacity, maximise total value when you may take fractions of items. Explain why a greedy by value-to-weight ratio is optimal here, contrast it with 0/1 Knapsack, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.

s1_definition.profdef: Fractional Knapsack maximises value within a weight capacity when items may be taken partially. The greedy strategy sorts items by value-to-weight ratio descending and fills the capacity with the densest items first, taking a fraction of the last item that only partly fits. Unlike 0/1 Knapsack, the fractional version is optimally solved greedily because partial selection removes the all-or-nothing obstacle.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India deploys a fixed amount of capital across investments that can be funded partially, and it funds the highest return-per-unit investments first to maximise total return.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sort by value per unit weight and fill greedily, splitting the last item if needed.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Fractional Knapsack maximises value within a weight capacity when items may be taken partially. The greedy strategy sorts items by value-to-weight ratio descending and fills the capacity with the densest items first, taking a fraction of the last item that only partly fits. Unlike 0/1 Knapsack, the fractional version is optimally solved greedily because partial selection removes the all-or-nothing obstacle.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India deploys a fixed amount of capital across investments that can be funded partially, and it funds the highest return-per-unit investments first to maximise total return.

**One line to remember:** Sort by value per unit weight and fill greedily, splitting the last item if needed.

sections.s2_technical:
We compute each item's value-to-weight ratio, its return per unit of capacity, and sort items by that ratio from highest to lowest. We then walk the sorted items, taking each one whole while it fits, subtracting its weight from the remaining capacity and adding its full value. When an item does not fully fit, we take the fraction that fills the remaining capacity, adding a proportional share of its value, and then the capacity is full and we stop. Because fractions are allowed, there is never a reason to skip a denser item in favour of a sparser one.

The greedy core is `sort by value/weight desc; for (Item it : items) { if (cap >= it.w) { cap -= it.w; total += it.v; } else { total += it.v * ((double) cap / it.w); break; } }`. A concrete check: with items of weight and value (10, 60), (20, 100), (30, 120) and capacity fifty, we take the first two whole and two-thirds of the third, for a total of two hundred forty. Senior nuance: this greedy is provably optimal only because of fractionality; the 0/1 version, where items are indivisible, defeats the greedy and requires dynamic programming. The cost is dominated by the sort at n log n.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India has a fixed amount of capital to deploy across several investment opportunities, each with an expected return and a capital requirement, and crucially each investment can be funded partially. The treasury team wants to maximise total expected return. Funding a low-density investment before a high-density one wastes capital. This is exactly how Fractional Knapsack works: fund the highest return-per-unit investments first, splitting the last one to exactly fill the capital.

The code defines a `CapitalDeploymentService` with `maxReturn(weights, values, capital)` using the ratio-sorted greedy. A `Demo` provides investments and logs the maximum return.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three investments needing capital ten, twenty, thirty with returns sixty, one hundred, one hundred twenty, and total capital fifty. Step 1: we compute return-per-capital ratios of six, five, and four. Step 2: we sort the investments descending by ratio, so the order is the ten-capital one, then the twenty-capital one, then the thirty-capital one. Step 3: we fund the densest investment fully, spending ten of the capital and gaining sixty, leaving forty. Step 4: we fund the next fully, spending twenty and gaining one hundred, leaving twenty. Step 5: the last investment needs thirty but only twenty remains, so we fund two-thirds of it, gaining two-thirds of one hundred twenty, which is eighty. Step 6: the total return is sixty plus one hundred plus eighty, which is two hundred forty, and we return that.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Fractional Knapsack is the problem where a greedy strategy is not just a heuristic but provably optimal, and the reason is the single word fractional. Because I am allowed to take a partial amount of any item, I compute each item's value-to-weight ratio, its return per unit of capacity, sort the items from the densest to the least dense, and simply fill the capacity from the top of that list. I take each item whole while it fits, and when I reach an item that only partly fits, I take exactly the fraction that fills the remaining capacity and add a proportional share of its value.

The contrast with 0/1 Knapsack is the point interviewers probe. In the 0/1 version items are indivisible, so the greedy by ratio can be wrong: a single dense but small item might block a pair of items that together fill the capacity more valuably, which is why that version needs dynamic programming. The moment fractions are permitted, that trap disappears, because any leftover capacity can always be filled with a slice of the next-densest item, so a simple exchange argument proves the ratio-sorted greedy optimal. The cost is dominated by the sort at n log n.

At the National Bank of India I used this to deploy a fixed capital pool across investment opportunities that could be funded partially, funding the highest return-per-capital opportunities first and taking a fraction of the last one to exactly exhaust the capital. Explaining the value-density sort, the partial fill of the final item, and precisely why fractionality makes the greedy optimal where the indivisible version needs dynamic programming is what shows an interviewer I understand both the greedy technique and its boundaries.
